name: Acute Limb Ischaemia

matching.reasoningTemplate: Sudden severe limb pain in a patient with an embolic source (atrial fibrillation) or peripheral arterial disease indicates acute limb ischaemia — a time-critical vascular emergency (the 6 Ps).

redFlags: Time-critical — irreversible tissue loss within ~6 h; pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia
Paralysis/anaesthesia (Rutherford IIb→III) → immediate revascularisation or the limb is lost
Systemic anticoagulate immediately unless contraindicated; urgent vascular referral

investigations.test: Handheld Doppler of distal pulses + ankle pressures
Urgent CT/MR/catheter angiography to localise occlusion

references: Harrison 22e — Vascular Diseases of the Extremities
provenanceNote: Recall Tier-4 (Group B) new diagnosable entity. AI-drafted; PENDING clinician sign-off. Uses only existing governed finding keys (no vocabulary change).

algorithms.title: Acute Limb Ischaemia: Diagnostic & Clinical Decision Pathway

steps.action: Evaluate acute presentation and core clinical features of Acute Limb Ischaemia.
Screen for high-risk signs: Time-critical - irreversible tissue loss within ~6 h; pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia
Targeted workup: Handheld Doppler of distal pulses + ankle pressures, Urgent CT/MR/catheter angiography to localise occlusion, ECG (atrial fibrillation), FBC, coagulation, group-and-save
Apply evidence-based criteria to classify disease severity and organ dysfunction.
Initiate guideline-directed medical therapy and monitor clinical progress.

valueTables.title: Recognising acute limb ischaemia and grading viability (Rutherford)

cells.text: Pain, pallor, paraesthesia, poikilothermia, pulselessness, paralysis
Pain may be out of proportion to findings
Onset within 14 days
Sudden fall in perfusion threatening the limb
Bifurcation just distal to the last palpable pulse
Rough bedside localisation
No sensory loss, no weakness
Arterial and venous Doppler audible; no immediate threat
None or minimal sensory loss (toes), no weakness
Arterial Doppler inaudible, venous audible; salvageable if treated promptly
Sensory loss beyond toes, mild to moderate weakness
{{hy:Salvageable only with immediate revascularisation}}
Profound anaesthesia, paralysis, rigor
Arterial and venous Doppler inaudible; major tissue loss
CT angiography first line; duplex or MRA if expertise
Must not delay heparin
ECG for atrial fibrillation, FBC, coagulation, group and save
Find embolic source and prepare for surgery

valueTables.title: Causes and mimics of acute limb ischaemia

cells.text: Cardiac or aortic source such as atrial fibrillation or aneurysm
Underlying atherosclerotic plaque or aneurysm
Chest or back pain with limb ischaemia
Tense tender compartment after trauma or reperfusion
Low cardiac output rather than a focal occlusion
Massive venous thrombosis with a swollen limb
Painful blue toes after angiography or stenting

valueTables.title: Management of acute limb ischaemia

cells.text: {{hy:As soon as ALI is suspected}}, unless contraindicated
75 units/kg IV bolus, then infusion with 4-hourly APTT; LMWH if infusion not feasible
All patients
Titrate oxygen to SpO2 above 96%
Occlusion under 2 weeks with intact motor and sensory function
tPA usually, over 4 to 24 h
Threatened limb; choice by severity and thrombus extent
Catheter or surgical
Unsuitable for catheter therapy
Depends on thrombus extent and patient condition
Compartment syndrome or after prolonged ischaemia
Watch for reperfusion hyperkalaemia, acidosis, myoglobinuria
Rutherford III
Senior team decision

valueTables.footnote: About 11% of treated patients still need amputation and 1-year mortality is about 40% (Merck). Thrombolytic dose is not stated in the sources opened.

flowcharts.title: Diagnosis and management of acute limb ischaemia

nodes.text: IV heparin bolus now; Doppler; ECG for AF
Grade I: urgent CT angiography and planned revascularisation
Grade IIa: urgent imaging, thrombolysis or thrombectomy
Grade III: primary amputation or palliation
